It closes the “shoreline infrastructure” gap with a named production asset rather than an invisible placeholder, a recycled generic puff, an unrelated object, or a crude primitive approximation. The result must communicate its purpose immediately through silhouette, motion, timing, optical response, state, surface contact, or interaction while following working-waterfront construction, salt exposure, wet timber, marine paint, galvanized hardware, rope, drainage, and practical repairs.

Required production anatomy: anchored base or mount, structural enclosure or frame, primary operating surface, user control or connection, service access, power, conduit, drainage, or network path, safety and weather protection, fasteners and identification. Every component is functional. Components connect through believable supports, timing relationships, strand roots, anatomy, attachment points, projection rules, emitter origins, service paths, collision-safe boundaries, or state transitions appropriate to Fishing Harbor shoreline Mooring Post Standard. Materials and response layers include painted or galvanized structure, service hardware, control or lens material, foundation or mounting material. Separation follows real construction, biological growth, light transport, contamination, weather, particle behavior, hair-fiber behavior, or gameplay state rather than arbitrary color blocks.

Implementation defines a stable named origin, deterministic forward or projection direction, scale envelope, spawn or placement conditions, looping or one-shot lifecycle, transition timing, cleanup and pooling, network relevance, quality tiers, editor-preview metadata, and validation thresholds. Dependencies on surfaces, bodies, vehicles, weapons, water, wind, camera, lighting, audio, quests, or interaction sockets are explicit and testable. Close-range presentation needs convincing breakup, thickness, depth, hardware, strand structure, species anatomy, or layered motion. Distant presentation preserves the primary read without excessive triangles, overdraw, alpha sorting, particle count, shadows, or replication traffic.

Fishing Harbor weather Stingray Standard is a dedicated-organic-rigging added by the final Zaylins gameplay, sensory, environmental, interaction, customization, and cohesion sweep for fishing-harbor. It closes the “weather creature” gap with a named production asset rather than an invisible placeholder, a recycled generic puff, an unrelated object, or a crude primitive approximation. The result must communicate its purpose immediately through silhouette, motion, timing, optical response, state, surface contact, or interaction while following working-waterfront construction, salt exposure, wet timber, marine paint, galvanized hardware, rope, drainage, and practical repairs.

Required production anatomy: continuous anatomical body, species-defining head, locomotion appendages, sensory features, mouth or feeding structure, skin, scale, shell, feather, or membrane system, root and animation hierarchy, habitat and schooling anchors. Every component is functional. Components connect through believable supports, timing relationships, strand roots, anatomy, attachment points, projection rules, emitter origins, service paths, collision-safe boundaries, or state transitions appropriate to Fishing Harbor weather Stingray Standard. Materials and response layers include species surface material, eyes and sensory material, appendage material, habitat-aware variation. Separation follows real construction, biological growth, light transport, contamination, weather, particle behavior, hair-fiber behavior, or gameplay state rather than arbitrary color blocks.

Implementation defines a stable named origin, deterministic forward or projection direction, scale envelope, spawn or placement conditions, looping or one-shot lifecycle, transition timing, cleanup and pooling, network relevance, quality tiers, editor-preview metadata, and validation thresholds. Dependencies on surfaces, bodies, vehicles, weapons, water, wind, camera, lighting, audio, quests, or interaction sockets are explicit and testable. Close-range presentation needs convincing breakup, thickness, depth, hardware, strand structure, species anatomy, or layered motion. Distant presentation preserves the primary read without excessive triangles, overdraw, alpha sorting, particle count, shadows, or replication traffic.

Accessibility is mandatory. The asset does not rely on color alone. Flashing, injury feedback, camera motion, particle density, and hazard communication include reduced-flash, reduced-motion, reduced-particle, high-contrast, or icon alternatives where relevant. Injury effects default to non-graphic presentation. Stylized blood is abstract and optional, contains no gore or exposed anatomy, and has paint, spark, dust, and comic-impact alternatives. Hair uses a scalp-conforming root field, purposeful hairline, believable density and gravity, style-specific structure, silhouette variation, ear and nape clearance, recolor support, and secondary-motion planning. Afros are not bunched spheres. Locs are not identical cylinders. Braids and twists show interwoven rhythm, parting, tension, taper, and purposeful styling.

This specification never authorizes crude geometry. Every layer reinforces Fishing Harbor weather Stingray Standard, integrates with adjacent Zaylins systems, and passes recognition, lifecycle, town-style, accessibility, performance, and state review. Specialized GLBs remain outside the generic primitive Blender lane until a dedicated builder can satisfy this contract.

Physical identity and semantic decision: the final category is vehicle because whole physical-object token resolves the asset as vehicle. Model it as a mechanically plausible transportation asset whose occupancy, cargo, propulsion, cooling, lighting, access, protection, and service systems are visually understandable. Words describing an animal, profession, customer, owner, district, collection, or story function may not force character or creature anatomy onto an object such as a cottage, boat, crate, display, station, rack, board, feeder, machine, sign, or piece of equipment. The named object must be identifiable in neutral clay material before labels, color, and glow are applied.

Silhouette and proportion: The transportation class must read from front, side, rear, and three-quarter views through stance, cabin or operator placement, overhangs, propulsion spacing, body volumes, glazing, and travel direction before decals or glow are considered. Keep the working envelope near 1.5 meters wide, 1.5 meters deep, and 1.5 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Boat Engine Stand; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Construction and functional anatomy: Include a load-bearing chassis or hull, occupant or cargo volume, access, controls, lighting, propulsion hardware, cooling or intake paths, service panels, energy connection, protected underside, and environment-specific safety systems. Required visible components are recognizable primary structure, functional secondary components, appropriate materials. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Materials, color, and lighting: use the named material vocabulary weathered wood, painted marine metal, rope, galvanized hardware, navy, cream, weathered red, teal, warm wood, galvanized metal. working coastal municipality; weathered wood, painted metal, rope, wet surfaces, practical marine hardware, salt-worn details. Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material. Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure. Avoid the town-specific failures: theme-park pirate props, clean plastic docks, empty decorative marina. Surface variation should follow manufacturing, age, handling, weather, moisture, heat, pressure, preparation, cleaning, or maintenance rather than random noise. Emissive areas must originate from a real lens, screen, fixture, projector, biological organ, or energy system.

Condition and environmental integration: Use salt exposure, sun fading, wet-darkened surfaces, rope polish, chipped marine paint, galvanized hardware, water staining near tide or wash zones, and practical repairs without turning every working asset into a wreck. Spawn it on a road, parking bay, rail, waterline, dock, garage, flight socket, or hover pad appropriate to the propulsion system. Preserve forward direction, idle stance, occupant entry, cargo or passenger clearance, turning or docking envelope, camera framing, and surrounding safety space. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Interaction and state design: Keep access panels, doors, lights, propulsion units, controls, cargo areas, steering surfaces, lift hardware, and service interfaces separately named for animation, customization, damage, maintenance, and gameplay states. Expected hooks include moving propulsion, steering, mechanism, or operating component. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use a stable chassis or hull collider with optional cabin, cargo, propulsion, or hit-region hulls. Do not trace every light, mirror, vent, wheel, pod, railing, rope, or fastener. Entry sockets and clearance volumes must align with the visible body. Use positive Z as forward and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the ground, waterline, rail, or hover-plane center below the chassis or hull, with separate transforms for propulsion and steering hardware. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Use sufficient geometry for reflective silhouette surfaces while economizing hidden undersides. Reuse repeated seats, lights, vents, wheels, pods, rails, and fasteners. LODs must preserve occupancy and propulsion logic. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 23,400 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 10,800 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 3,600 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: The transportation class must read from front, side, rear, and three-quarter views through stance, cabin or operator placement, overhangs, propulsion spacing, body volumes, glazing, and travel direction before decals or glow are considered.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. A technically valid file that looks generic, toy-like, structurally impossible, context-free, semantically misclassified, or unlike Boat Engine Stand is a failure. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.

Expected hooks include seating, occupancy, or interaction sockets. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use one or more primitive or low-complexity hulls matching the major blocking volume and interaction surface. Decorative handles, cables, slats, fasteners, trim, lenses, foliage, and surface detail must not create snagging collision. Use positive Z as the front or primary use direction and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the ground contact, wall mount, suspension point, waterline, or logical placement center. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Keep ergonomic silhouette and contact points at every LOD. Repeated slats, legs, buttons, cushions, shelves, and fasteners should share meshes or instances. Far output should target roughly 2,160 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: Seat or work height, depth, back angle, leg clearance, storage volume, support placement, and reachable controls must immediately explain how a person uses the object.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. Physical identity and semantic decision: the final category is vehicle because strong filename prefix resolves the physical object as vehicle. Model it as a mechanically plausible transportation asset whose occupancy, cargo, propulsion, cooling, lighting, access, protection, and service systems are visually understandable. Words describing an animal, profession, customer, owner, district, collection, or story function may not force character or creature anatomy onto an object such as a cottage, boat, crate, display, station, rack, board, feeder, machine, sign, or piece of equipment. The named object must be identifiable in neutral clay material before labels, color, and glow are applied.

Silhouette and proportion: The transportation class must read from front, side, rear, and three-quarter views through stance, cabin or operator placement, overhangs, propulsion spacing, body volumes, glazing, and travel direction before decals or glow are considered. Keep the working envelope near 1.5 meters wide, 1.5 meters deep, and 1.5 meters high. Only reviewed protrusions such as signs, arms, doors, mirrors, roots, branches, railings, hoses, lighting, propulsion, awnings, stairs, or service hardware may extend beyond it. Every major and secondary form must reinforce Harbor Skiff; unrelated decorative mass should be removed.

Construction and functional anatomy: Include a load-bearing chassis or hull, occupant or cargo volume, access, controls, lighting, propulsion hardware, cooling or intake paths, service panels, energy connection, protected underside, and environment-specific safety systems. Required visible components are recognizable primary structure, functional secondary components, appropriate materials. Each one must connect through credible frames, joints, seams, foundations, roots, brackets, fasteners, cables, pipes, glazing frames, hinges, biological attachment, serving structure, packaging, or material transitions. Flat paint, decals, and emission may not replace a component that explains operation, weight support, access, occupancy, growth, containment, drainage, power, preparation, protection, or maintenance.

Materials, color, and lighting: use the named material vocabulary weathered wood, painted marine metal, rope, galvanized hardware, navy, cream, weathered red, teal, warm wood, galvanized metal. working coastal municipality; weathered wood, painted metal, rope, wet surfaces, practical marine hardware, salt-worn details. Metal surfaces need distinct painted, powder-coated, galvanized, brushed, cast, polished, oxidized, or heat-affected responses rather than one universal gray material. Glass requires thickness, framing, tint appropriate to the town, controlled transparency, believable roughness, and an interior or backing surface so it does not read as an empty blue plane. Stone, brick, concrete, plaster, stucco, tile, and asphalt should show scale-correct joints, aggregate or surface breakup, edge wear, drainage staining, and construction transitions without noisy procedural speckling. Wood needs believable board direction, grain scale, end grain, joinery, sealing, wear, and moisture response appropriate to indoor, residential, marine, fantasy, or industrial use. Fabric, upholstery, leather, rubber, and flexible polymers require thickness, seams, compression or tension cues, stitching where visible, and roughness variation tied to handling. Emissive accents must arise from a lens, strip, screen, projector, fixture, biological organ, or energy component. Do not paint unexplained neon lines across ordinary structure. Avoid the town-specific failures: theme-park pirate props, clean plastic docks, empty decorative marina. Surface variation should follow manufacturing, age, handling, weather, moisture, heat, pressure, preparation, cleaning, or maintenance rather than random noise. Emissive areas must originate from a real lens, screen, fixture, projector, biological organ, or energy system.

Condition and environmental integration: Use salt exposure, sun fading, wet-darkened surfaces, rope polish, chipped marine paint, galvanized hardware, water staining near tide or wash zones, and practical repairs without turning every working asset into a wreck. Spawn it on a road, parking bay, rail, waterline, dock, garage, flight socket, or hover pad appropriate to the propulsion system. Preserve forward direction, idle stance, occupant entry, cargo or passenger clearance, turning or docking envelope, camera framing, and surrounding safety space. Add contact shadows, foundations, feet, brackets, roots, piles, seals, trim, drainage, terrain blending, waterline response, or wall transitions where the object meets its environment. It may not appear pasted into the scene or suspended by invisible support unless the design explicitly includes a justified force, mount, cable, lift field, or suspension system.

Interaction and state design: Keep access panels, doors, lights, propulsion units, controls, cargo areas, steering surfaces, lift hardware, and service interfaces separately named for animation, customization, damage, maintenance, and gameplay states. Expected hooks include moving propulsion, steering, mechanism, or operating component, seating, occupancy, or interaction sockets. Separate and name parts that can open, slide, rotate, illuminate, display content, receive an item, carry an occupant, change material, emit particles, take damage, be repaired, be harvested, or connect to another system. Static detail should remain efficient, but useful gameplay state boundaries may not be merged away.

Collision, orientation, and export: Use a stable chassis or hull collider with optional cabin, cargo, propulsion, or hit-region hulls. Do not trace every light, mirror, vent, wheel, pod, railing, rope, or fastener. Entry sockets and clearance volumes must align with the visible body. Use positive Z as forward and positive Y as up after export conversion. Place the origin at the ground, waterline, rail, or hover-plane center below the chassis or hull, with separate transforms for propulsion and steering hardware. Use one named asset root, semantically named render meshes, separate animated or stateful parts, simplified collision, and metadata for asset ID, town, family, source document, license, dimensions, final semantic category, and specification version. Remove preview cameras, lights, helpers, unused materials, duplicates, hidden placeholders, and accidental geometry before GLB export.

Performance and LOD: Use sufficient geometry for reflective silhouette surfaces while economizing hidden undersides. Reuse repeated seats, lights, vents, wheels, pods, rails, and fasteners. LODs must preserve occupancy and propulsion logic. Close-range output may use up to the reviewed maximum, with a practical target near 23,400 triangles when silhouette and required components justify it. Medium-range output should target roughly 10,800 triangles while preserving primary form, supports, interaction components, openings, material blocks, and essential lights. Far output should target roughly 3,600 triangles or a suitable impostor while retaining the recognizable outline, mounting or ground relationship, and major color or emissive signature. Reduction may never destroy this recognition requirement: The transportation class must read from front, side, rear, and three-quarter views through stance, cabin or operator placement, overhangs, propulsion spacing, body volumes, glazing, and travel direction before decals or glow are considered.

Acceptance standard: the final model must look intentional from every inspection angle, satisfy every required component, fit the reviewed scale, use meaningful material separation, remain inside geometry budgets, sit correctly on its placement plane, and export as a verified nonempty GLB. A technically valid file that looks generic, toy-like, structurally impossible, context-free, semantically misclassified, or unlike Harbor Skiff is a failure. Correct it, retry it, or quarantine it instead of publishing it.
